segment:
The man’s heartbeat had barely changed at all during the night. She caught herself glancing toward her chest and quickly averted her eyes, as though to check her pulse would give away some secret.
He paused at the bottom of the steps and offered his hand. She felt a faint trembling in her own hands. Her right palm was sweaty. She slid her left into the soft leather and gripped his hand. He squeezed hers back: a handshake between friends or business partners, nothing more.
She took a deep breath. “Good night,” she said, her voice cracking slightly. “I’ll see you tomorrow.”
“I suppose so,” Jonah said. The dark eyes narrowed, almost closed, and the corners of the mouth turned up. It could have been amusement, or maybe surprise. She couldn’t tell. “Are you going to be all right, Mara?”
She cleared her throat, but the voice was still hoarse when it came out. “Oh, I’ll be fine.” Her left hand trembled again in his grasp. She felt like a kid who’d just learned how to shake hands: the thumb and forefinger pressed down tight as she forced herself not to squeeze his hand back. He squeezed hers. “You should go, Jonah. I’m going to have to walk back to the hotel alone.”
“Alone?” he said. There was something like concern on his face now, as though he thought she were in danger. Her heart skipped a beat at the thought.
“Of course,” she said. “I’m not going to stay with you all night.” She felt a blush creeping up her neck and cheeks. It would be obvious in the soft moonlight, no doubt. “It’s a long walk. I’d rather not do it alone.” She could feel her left hand tightening around his again. She swallowed hard and forced it to relax.
“I don’t mind,” Jonah said, looking up at her. He was smiling slightly. The corners of the mouth twitched. “But I suppose that’s up to you.” His gaze dropped to the sidewalk, where he continued staring. It was nearly two miles back to the hotel, she thought. He hadn’t said he would follow her. Hadn’t even asked if he could. He would walk home, and she would walk home, and it might be several days or weeks before they saw each other again.
Her right hand rose almost on its own. “Wait,” she said. Her breath came out in a short gasp, but she couldn’t stop herself. There was nothing else for it now, though, was there?
His left hand turned palm down, and his fingers brushed hers briefly. She swallowed again. The trembling started in her hands and spread to her legs and back, until she was shaking all over. He stood stock-still; the only movement came from his eyes as they moved between her face and the sidewalk. The darkness beyond the front gate was thick and close, blotting out the distant street lamps that gleamed like tiny stars.
text:
They started at Fulcrum’s front steps, an instant after the last of the lab staff had gone indoors and locked up. Mara’s mouth felt raw and dry; her throat ached, and her shoulders were rigid and aching too. Her entire body was too hot despite the cold, and she didn’t feel the chill of the night air.
The others were gone. Jonah stood silently beside her, waiting. He was six inches taller than she was. He wasn’t looking at her; his head turned toward the empty drive, and he stared into the darkness beyond the lighted entrance. There was nothing there. She didn’t look. She watched him instead.
“I guess it’s time to go home.” Jonah’s voice was soft, almost inaudible. She had expected more after tonight: analysis or commiseration. Instead he turned sideways with a small sigh and started down the front steps. He swung both arms easily, as though he were on an ordinary walk, though it was the middle of the night and they were both on their way back to hotel rooms in a town she didn’t know.
She followed, trying to match his step. His dark hair rustled as he moved, a low whisper that went with the sound of his breathing: slow, even, no sign of anxiety.

segment:
His shirt was open to the waist and caught faintly on his skin like the edge of a spiderweb, a tiny sound beneath the larger sounds of his feet, his breath. It was enough to keep her focused.
Jonah turned his head to the sky as he walked. There were stars. He looked at them for a while, and when he turned back, his eyes passed over hers, without stopping or focusing. His hair lay flat against his neck and temples in the cold night air. The black of it was darker than his shadow. His left hand shifted along the hem of his shirt, once, and stopped there. He was a silent dark line ahead of her. His head turned back to look at the stars, and she watched him looking.
Jonah stopped, a few paces from her. “Are you okay?” The question was quiet and serious, but when he turned, there was no worry on his face. She saw no signs of it in his body or his hands. He didn’t wait for her to answer. She looked at him until his gaze drifted down into her face. His eyes rested for a moment in the hollow where her throat met her neck. His hand was near his hip. There was no tension in his posture, but he held his weight evenly on both feet. He didn’t seem impatient, or anxious to leave.
She heard a sudden movement behind her and stopped walking. She felt Jonah’s gaze pass over her again and return, and she turned her head to watch him.
The shadow of a van crossed the drive in front of them as it turned around on the road. Its tail lights disappeared; its doors slammed. Mara’s shoulders tensed, and she heard herself exhale without knowing how much breath had gathered in her chest. Her armpits prickled; she felt an itch below one of her ribs, but didn’t move. Her eyes went to Jonah’s face. He watched her with no expression but waiting. Her back and thighs tightened together again as her legs turned and she continued walking after him.
His hands came loose from his hips and he slowed as he went. The cold wind ruffled the hair at the back of his neck; his shirt caught faintly on his skin again. Mara saw his knuckles lighten as his fingers spread and closed on his shirtsleeve, but there was no force in the movement. Her head felt light. She stopped walking and tried to focus on her breath. The air came in through her nostrils, cool and thin on her tongue. Her eyes rested on Jonah’s back as she forced herself to breathe.

segment:
His clothing rustled too: plain black shirt and pants, standard issue for an agent who needed to move unnoticed. If he hadn’t been six and a half feet tall.
Jonah stopped in front of her at the bottom of the stairs, blocking her way. She walked into his shadow. Her heart throbbed in her throat; her pulse fluttered like a trapped bird.
He still wasn’t looking at her, but when she reached him, he held out a hand without saying a word. Mara had known he would do it. It was the right thing to do. That didn’t make it easier to refuse.
She looked at his palm: bare, callused and warm.
He was tall, but he wasn’t too tall to touch her. She leaned up and pressed her cheek into the warm curve of his shoulder; she felt the smooth cotton of his shirt. Her face was hot again. She breathed in hard: he smelled like woodsmoke and clean rain.
He reached past her shoulder, still without looking at her. His hand cupped the nape of her neck.
“You did all right, Mara,” he said, voice soft, so soft. “You were brave tonight. Don’t be scared.”
Her heart stopped. Her whole body stopped, still as a statue: a girl on a hill. A frozen moment.
She knew the story. She knew he didn’t mean it. Still she hesitated. For the first time in two years she hesitated. Her body stayed still when her mind said go.
Jonah shifted his grip, his palm warm against her neck. He was so much taller than she was: he had to lean down to kiss her.
Mara closed her eyes and lifted her face. His breath moved warm and heavy against her lips. His mouth was cool. She couldn’t remember the last time she had touched someone. She put both hands on his chest. The fabric of his shirt was a thin barrier between them.
He kissed her again. Mara tasted him, and her eyes flew open. There was a sharp clean taste of rain, woodsmoke and dust.
She lifted a hand to cup his face. Her fingertips moved through the cool damp silk of his hair. He let out a low, slow breath and stopped moving, his weight solid against hers. She felt the small shudder of his shoulders; his breathing changed, deeper and slower.
It felt good to touch. Mara lifted her head to meet his mouth again, to let her hand slide over his jaw and then lower, into the curve of his neck.
He was still. No move. No protest. She hesitated a heartbeat and pulled his shirt open, unfastening the top buttons one by one. His bare skin was cool under her fingertips.

segment:
His back was straight as a rod; one side of his jaw ticked rhythmically as though he were chewing something.
At the bottom of the stairs, she touched his arm as though asking permission to walk alongside him. “Thanks for this,” she said quietly, looking away. “For…tonight. For everything.”
He nodded slightly, his body still turned away from her.
“No.” He took her hand instead of returning the touch. “Thank you, Mara.”
She let herself be led into the night.

They walked a little faster along the street; the cold air did nothing to lower the heat that still crawled in her head. She was hungry, but she didn’t care; she wanted the heat to go away and leave her body alone. Jonah’s hand stayed where it was: his fingers tangled with hers, warm, close to her heartbeat. She stared ahead, trying to read the signs on buildings, but they were too dark or too hard to focus on. A couple of people went past in the opposite direction. She saw a homeless person huddled in a doorway; they walked by silently.
It wasn’t far to the hotel. Mara felt a prickle of static across her skin as she crossed the street. The city was quieter now, no more traffic. Jonah let go of her hand, and the sudden cold made her flinch; her grip on his arm tightened and she pulled him back a little.
He stopped, surprised. His face was pale in the light from a streetlamp, the outline of his lips almost lost in shadow.
“You okay?” She meant to ask if he’d been hurt before, tonight, but her voice came out as a whisper.
“I…”
There was nothing between them—just the darkness of a narrow space in an alley behind some businesses that had closed for the night. He looked away and then back at her, his eyes dark and thoughtful. She felt like an object he had noticed in the night’s background and had only now chosen to look at seriously. He took her hand again; his fingertips moved gently over hers as if touching the surface of water.
“Are you?” she asked. “Really?”
She could feel him hesitate. His breath was warmer than the cold air; she could see the mist from his exhaled words, like smoke from an extinguished candle.
He opened his mouth to speak but stopped, as though unsure what to say. Instead, he lifted his other hand and touched her cheek gently. She leaned forward without thinking, into his palm. His fingers were soft as silk against her skin.
When she stopped, his hand fell away from her face.
“I’m fine,” she said quickly, not wanting him to see that she wasn’t.
He watched her for a moment, his expression unreadable. He pulled away and started walking again, faster than before; she followed, still holding his hand.
